title: Overlapping labels
objectives: Weight samples by how unique their labels are.
Compute the effective number of labels and an honest standard error for a hit rate.

screens.title: Labels that share days
screens.prose: Four triple-barrier labels over ten days. Each bar runs from its entry day to its first touch. Label A depends on days 0 to 3, label B on days 2 to 5, and so on.
screens.question: Tap every day that more than one label depends on.

hints.text: Look down each day's column and count the bars above it.
A and B overlap here.
A and B share days 2 and 3; B and C share days 4 and 5. Day 7 has no label at all.

feedback.correct: Days 2 to 5 each carry two labels.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the bars over each day; keep the days with two or more.

byKey.ab: You found A and B's overlap. B and C overlap too, on days 4 and 5.
byKey.c6: Day 6 carries only C; B ended on day 5.
byKey.c7: Day 7 has no label over it at all.

explain.text: Days 2 to 5 sit under two bars each. What happens on day 3 moves both A and B, so those two labels are partly the same evidence. Counting A and B as two independent trades overstates what we know.

screens.title: How much of each label is its own?
screens.prose: The array now shows $c_t$, the number of labels covering day $t$: the **concurrency**. On a day shared by two labels, each owns half of it, $1/c_t$. A label's **average uniqueness** is the mean of $1/c_t$ over its days.
screens.question: Fill in the average uniqueness of each label, to 4 places.

hints.text: For A: days 0 to 3 have $c_t = 1, 1, 2, 2$.
Read C's days here.
A: $(1 + 1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac12)/4 = 0.75$. B: $\tfrac12$ throughout. C: $(\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + 1)/3 = 0.6667$. D: 1.

feedback.correct: A 0.75, B 0.5, C 0.6667, D 1: together 2.92 labels' worth of evidence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average $1/c_t$ over each label's own days, including the shared ones.

explain.text: B shares every one of its days, so it is worth half a label. D shares none, so it is worth a whole one. The four labels add up to $2.9167$ independent labels, not 4.

screens.title: Concurrency in code

screens.question: Complete `concurrency` so it returns $c_t$ for every day.

hints.text: Both ends are included, so the window has `e - s + 1` days.
`range(s, e + 1)` stops after `e`.
Inside the loop: `for t in range(s, e + 1): c[t] += 1`.

screens.title: Uniqueness in code
screens.prose: This is López de Prado's **sample uniqueness**, from *Advances in Financial Machine Learning*. Each label gets a weight: the mean of $1/c_t$ over its own days. Code it on top of `concurrency`.
screens.question: Complete `average_uniqueness` so it returns one weight per label, rounded to 4 places.

widget.solution:
def average_uniqueness(starts, ends, n_days):
    c = concurrency(starts, ends, n_days)
    weights = []
    for s, e in zip(starts, ends):
        u = sum(1 / c[t] for t in range(s, e + 1)) / (e - s + 1)
        weights.append(round(u, 4))
    return weights

hints.text: A label covering days `s` to `e` has `e - s + 1` days.
This is the answer for the four labels.
`u = sum(1 / c[t] for t in range(s, e + 1)) / (e - s + 1)`.

feedback.correct: Each weight is the share of its days a label owns.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average $1/c_t$ over the label's days only, both ends included.

explain.text: On the seeded series the 971 weights average 0.161. About six labels cover a typical day. AFML also scales each weight by the size of the label's return; we keep to uniqueness.

screens.title: How many labels, really?
screens.prose: The seeded series has 971 triple-barrier labels. The chart shows their average uniqueness. The mean weight is 0.1606. The sum of the weights is the **effective number** of labels: how many independent ones they are worth.
screens.question: What is the effective number of labels?

hints.text: The sum of the weights is the count times the mean.
Most labels sit here.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of labels by the mean weight.

byKey.n: That counts every label as a whole one. Each owns about a sixth of its days.
byKey.inv: You divided by the mean weight. Multiply: overlap shrinks the sample.

explain.text: 971 labels carry about 156 labels' worth of independent evidence, a sixth. That is the $n$ any standard error should use. Lesson 12 of limits-thm asked how many trades skill needs; overlap moves that target out of reach faster.

screens.title: A hit rate four standard errors up
screens.prose: With a 20-day limit, 57.1% of the series' 961 labels hit the profit barrier. A colleague writes: "standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n} = 1.6\%$, so we are 4.5 standard errors above 50%." The labels' uniqueness weights sum to 140.
screens.question: How strong is the evidence?

options.text: Weak: with $n \approx 140$ the se is about 4.2%, under 2 se above 50%

options.why: You used $n = 961$. The labels overlap so much they are worth about 140; the se grows by $\sqrt{961/140}$.

options.text: Stronger than it looks: overlap means each result was confirmed many times
options.why: Overlapping labels repeat the same price moves. Repetition is not confirmation.

options.text: No evidence at all, because overlapping labels are invalid
options.why: The labels are fine as labels. Only the count of independent ones shrinks.

hints.text: Which $n$ belongs in $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$?
The naive interval is this narrow.
$\sqrt{0.572 \times 0.428 / 140} \approx 0.042$, so the hit rate is about 1.7 se above 50%.

feedback.correct: About 1.7 standard errors: suggestive, not proof.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recompute the standard error with the effective number of labels.

byKey.naive: You used all 961 labels as independent. They are worth about 140, so the se is 4.2%, not 1.6%.

explain.text: With the uniqueness weights, the hit rate is 0.572 and its se 0.042, on about 140 effective labels. That is 1.7 se above 50%, not 4.5. Stat-learning lesson 14 warned the same: $n$ is not what it looks like.

screens.title: An honest standard error in code
screens.prose: Weight each label by its uniqueness. The weighted hit rate counts a shared label as part of one. The effective $n$ is the sum of the weights. Then $\text{se} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n_{\text{eff}}}$.
screens.question: Complete `effective_n` and `weighted_hit_rate_se`.

tests.setup: starts, ends, labels, n = label_windows(21, 2, 20); u = average_uniqueness(starts, ends, n)
starts, ends, labels, n = label_windows(21, 2, 20); u = average_uniqueness(starts, ends, n)
tests.call: weighted_hit_rate_se([1 if y == 1 else 0 for y in labels], u)

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: short lists and the 20-day-limit labels of `label_windows(21, 2, 20)`. Their weights come from `average_uniqueness`; both functions are already defined. Each number is compared with math.isclose. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: With all weights 1 these are the usual hit rate and se.
Here B, weight 0.5, is the only miss.
`p = sum(w * h for w, h in zip(weights, hits)) / n_eff` and `se = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n_eff)`.

feedback.correct: With weights 1 you recover the textbook formula; with overlap the se grows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the weighted hits by the sum of the weights, and use that sum as $n$.

explain.text: The third and fourth tests differ only in the weights: 0.1 each makes $n_{\text{eff}} = 10$, and the se grows $\sqrt{10}$ times. The weighted hit rate barely moves; its uncertainty is what changes. That is overlap's main cost.

screens.title: Putting the weights to work
screens.prose: The weights also go into training. scikit-learn's `fit(X, y, sample_weight=w)` makes a shared label count for less. A bagged model can draw its bootstrap rows with probability proportional to $w$. AFML's **sequential bootstrap** goes further and draws rows that overlap little with those already drawn.
screens.question: Why does a plain bootstrap of overlapping rows mislead a random forest?

options.text: Its samples are full of near-copies, so the trees look more different and more certain than the data allow

options.why: A bootstrap draws as many rows as there are. The problem is which rows: heavily shared ones are treated as fresh.
A forest ignores order inside a sample anyway. Overlap, not order, is the trouble.

options.text: It does not: each tree sees a random sample
options.why: Random over rows is not random over independent evidence. Overlapping rows are drawn as if they were.

hints.text: What does a bootstrap assume about its rows?
D owns all its days; B owns half.
It assumes they are independent. Overlapping labels are not, so each sample repeats the same price moves.

feedback.correct: The bootstrap assumes independent rows; overlap breaks that.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what a bootstrap assumes about its rows.

explain.text: A plain bootstrap gives each row the same chance, so heavily shared stretches are drawn many times. The weighted draw favours unique labels: D comes up twice as often as B. Ensembles lesson 7's out-of-bag scores suffer the same way, as left-out rows have near-copies in the bag.

screens.title: One label over everything
screens.prose: Four labels on ten days: A covers days 0 to 9, a time-out. B covers only day 0, C only day 5 and D only day 9. Each is a touch on the next close. So $c_t = 2$ on days 0, 5 and 9, and 1 elsewhere.
screens.question: What is the average uniqueness of A?

hints.text: Average $1/c_t$ over all ten of A's days.
Three of A's days are shared.

feedback.correct: A owns 85% of its days; B, C and D own half of theirs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average over all ten days of A.

byKey.half: That is B's weight: its only day is shared. A shares just 3 of its 10 days.
byKey.one: A shares days 0, 5 and 9, so it cannot be fully unique.

explain.text: A is worth 0.85 of a label, and B, C and D 0.5 each: 2.35 in all. The short labels are halved by one long neighbour. With no overlap at all every weight would be 1, and nothing would change.

screens.title: Uniqueness and the effective sample
screens.prose: For label $i$ with window $[s_i, e_i]$: $$c_t = \#\{j : s_j \le t \le e_j\}, \qquad \bar u_i = \frac{1}{e_i - s_i + 1}\sum_{t=s_i}^{e_i} \frac{1}{c_t}, \qquad n_{\text{eff}} = \sum_i \bar u_i.$$ A hit rate's se uses $n_{\text{eff}}$.
screens.question: Ten labels never overlap. What is $n_{\text{eff}}$?

options.text: 10: every $c_t$ is 1, so every weight is 1

options.why: That would be one label covering everything alone. Separate windows each own all their days.

options.text: Less than 10, because the labels are short
options.why: Length does not matter; sharing does. With $c_t = 1$ throughout, each weight is 1.

hints.text: Put $c_t = 1$ into $\bar u_i$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no overlap, what is $c_t$ on a labelled day?

explain.text: Without overlap $c_t = 1$ on every labelled day, so $\bar u_i = 1$ and $n_{\text{eff}} = n$. The correction only bites when labels share days. Trading once every $h$ days gives that, at the price of far fewer labels.

screens.title: 2,000 trades, or 180?
screens.prose: A research note claims "a 53% hit rate on 2,000 labelled trades, $t = 2.7$". The trades are daily entries with triple-barrier labels lasting about 11 days. Their uniqueness weights sum to 180.
screens.question: What is the $t$ statistic with the effective $n$?

hints.text: The se uses $n = 180$ now.
The row to fill.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recompute the se with $n = 180$, then divide 0.03 by it.

byKey.claimed: That is the note's own figure, with $n = 2{,}000$.
byKey.ratio: You scaled $t$ by $180/2000$. The se scales with $\sqrt{n}$, so $t$ falls by $\sqrt{2000/180} \approx 3.3$.

explain.text: The se grows by $\sqrt{2000/180} \approx 3.33$, from 1.12% to 3.72%. So $t$ falls from 2.69 to 0.81: well inside what luck gives. The note has about 180 trades' worth of evidence, and should say so.

ideas: A triple-barrier label depends on the days from entry to first touch, so neighbouring labels share days.
Average uniqueness, the mean of $1/c_t$ over a label's days, weights each label by the evidence it owns.
The sum of the weights is the effective $n$: use it for standard errors, sample weights and bootstraps.

formula.name: Average uniqueness
formula.note: $n_{\text{eff}} = \sum_i \bar u_i$; with no overlap every $\bar u_i = 1$.

summary.trap: A hit rate's standard error computed with every overlapping label as independent is several times too small.

quiz.prose: Triple-barrier labels with a 20-day limit. Most labels touch a barrier within 8 days. A colleague purges every training label whose window overlaps the test block. They use each label's first-touch day as its end.
quiz.question: Is that purge right?

options.text: Yes: a label depends on its entry to its first touch, so that is the window to purge on
No: it must always use the full 20 days
options.why: Purging on 20 days is safe but throws away labels that ended long before the test block.

options.text: No: use a fixed 8 days for every label
options.why: A fixed 8 days cuts short every label that ran longer, and those leak into the test block.

feedback.correct: Purge on each label's real window.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which days does a triple-barrier label actually depend on?

explain.text: Validation lesson 7 purged training labels whose windows overlap the test block. For triple-barrier labels the window is entry to first touch, different for each label. A fixed shorter span leaks; the full limit is safe but wasteful.

quiz.prose: Two labels cover days 0 to 4 and days 0 to 4: the same window.
quiz.question: What is each label's average uniqueness?

feedback.correct: Identical windows split the evidence in half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every day is shared by both.

byKey.one: You counted each label as unique. They share every day, so each owns half.

explain.text: Every day has $c_t = 2$, so each label's weight is $\tfrac12$ and $n_{\text{eff}} = 1$. Two copies of one bet are one bet.

quiz.prose: A researcher bootstraps the 961 overlapping labels, resampling rows independently. They report a 95% interval for the hit rate of ±3.2 points.
quiz.question: What is wrong with the interval?

options.text: It is too narrow: resampling rows as if independent ignores that neighbours share outcomes
It is too wide: overlap adds information
options.why: Overlap repeats information; it never adds it.

options.text: Nothing: the bootstrap needs no assumptions
options.why: The plain bootstrap assumes independent rows, which overlapping labels are not.

feedback.correct: An independent-row bootstrap inherits the naive $n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does a row bootstrap assume?

explain.text: ±3.2 points matches the naive se of 1.6%. With about 140 effective labels the honest interval is about ±8 points. A block bootstrap, or weights, respects the overlap.

quiz.prose: Labels cover days 1 to 3, 2 to 6 and 3 to 4.
quiz.question: What is $c_3$?

feedback.correct: Day 3 is inside all three windows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each window for day 3, ends included.

byKey.two: Both ends count: the first window ends on day 3 and the third starts there.

explain.text: Windows 1 to 3, 2 to 6 and 3 to 4 all contain day 3, so $c_3 = 3$. Ends are included because the label depends on that day's close.
